newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: FOCUS-Pakistan budget aims to boost economy.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Pakistan budget aims to boost economy.

text.p: Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif's government on Friday unveiled a budget he said would stimulate the ailing economy and curb a chronic fiscal deficit without imposing new taxes.
The first response of the business community to the budget for fiscal 1997/98 (July/June), announced in parliament by Finance Minister Sartaj Aziz, was positive.
But opposition leader Benazir Bhutto attacked the measure as designed to benefit foreign investors at the expense of local industry and consumers.

The budget, the first of Sharif's 16-week-old government, allocated 134 billion rupees ($3.3 billion) for defence out of total expenditure of 552 billion rupees. It was a two percent nominal increase over last year, but a decrease in real terms after inflation that is now running at about 13 percent.
Pakistan, long at odds with India, is due to host a new round of talks between top foreign ministry officials next Thursday designed to reduce political and military tension with its giant neighbour.
The total budget outlay of 552 billion rupees represents an increase of 10.4 percent over last year's 500.2 billion.

Aziz told Reuters Financial Television that apart from debt servicing, he would curb all areas of spending, including defence, to cut the budget deficit to five percent of gross domestic product from this year's 6.2 percent.

"We have continued this policy for the next year to keep a very strong curb on the other expenditure, and that includes defence expenditure," he said. "We are now focusing on the revival of the economy."
"These are our four critical targets: seven percent industrial growth, five percent agricultural growth, six percent GDP growth, and 15 percent export growth."

In his budget speech, Aziz estimated revenues at 487.4 billion rupees compared to the spendings of 552 billion rupees, leaving a gap of 64.6 billion rupees which he said would be partly met by bank borrowing of about 55 billion.

The remaining gap of 9.8 billion rupees would be filled by additional revenues of 6.2 billion expected from tax reforms without imposinbg new taxes and 3.6 billion rupees from additional profit from the state telecommunications utility.
Inflation could be cut to single figures in 1997/98 if production picked up and money supply was restrained, he said.
"This is a budget of disinformation and deceit. This is shocking," Bhutto told reporters soon after Aziz's speech in which he blamed her previous government for creating an economic crisis.

Bhutto, whose government was dismissed by President Farooq Leghari in November on disputed charges of corruption and misrule, said tax and tariff cuts would benefit the rich and foreign investors and hit the local industry. "It amounts to bribing Western producers."
Karachi Stock Exchange president Arif Habib said: "Overall the budget is in line with (the) market's expectations. There are no big surprises, positive or negative."
"The budget is very constructive and very good," Karachi Cotton Association chairman Nadershaw Kabraji said.
"Low taxes, political stability and consistency in government's policies will certain encourage foreign investment," Deutsche Bank country manager Younus Khan said.
